options.a: Fill it at once, since a fax from a known prescriber needs no further validity check
options.b: Verify prescriber authenticity per state law and pharmacy policy before filling
options.c: Ask the patient to bring the original paper copy before dispensing any of the drug
options.d: Accept it only for hospice or long-term care patients, as with Schedule II faxes

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes a known prescriber removes the need to validate a faxed order; state rules still require confirming it is authentic.
distractorExplanations.c: Faxed non-controlled prescriptions are valid in most states; demanding the paper original confuses faxes with Schedule II rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Borrows the Schedule II fax exceptions (hospice, LTCF, home infusion); a non-controlled faxed order is not limited that way.

options.a: Fill it now, since Schedule III refills may be dispensed any time within six months
options.b: Refuse it, because Schedule III prescriptions cannot carry refills under federal law
options.c: Review refill date, check early refill rules, and consult pharmacist if outside allowed window
options.d: Fill it early if the patient pays cash, since early-refill limits apply to insurance claims

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the six-month validity window for C-III refills with permission to refill at any time; early fills still need review.
distractorExplanations.b: Applies the Schedule II no-refill rule to Schedule III; C-III to C-V allow up to five refills within six months.
distractorExplanations.d: Paying cash does not lift controlled-substance refill rules; early-refill limits are legal and clinical, not only payer edits.

options.a: Patient name, drug name, diagnosis code, insurance group number, and technician initials
options.b: Drug name/strength, directions, NDC barcode, and lot number, with patient name optional
options.c: Patient name, directions, manufacturer address, wholesale price, and the DEA schedule symbol
options.d: Patient name, drug name/strength, directions, prescriber, pharmacy contact, and Rx number

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnosis codes and insurance group numbers are billing data, not required label elements; it also omits strength and prescriber.
distractorExplanations.b: Patient name is a mandatory label element; NDC barcodes and lot numbers are inventory data, not required on the patient label.
distractorExplanations.c: Manufacturer address and wholesale price are not label requirements; the label must show strength, prescriber, and pharmacy details.

options.a: Dispense both, since duplicate ACE inhibitor alerts are informational only
options.b: Call the prescriber yourself to choose which ACE inhibitor to discontinue
options.c: Notify the pharmacist for clinical review before dispensing
options.d: Override the alert after confirming both drugs came from different prescribers

distractorExplanations.a: Therapeutic duplication alerts are clinical safety flags, not informational notices; two ACE inhibitors need pharmacist review.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong party: resolving therapeutic duplication with the prescriber is a pharmacist's clinical task, not a technician's.
distractorExplanations.d: Different prescribers make duplication more likely, not acceptable; technicians do not override clinical alerts.

options.a: 10 days
options.b: 15 days
options.c: 28 days
options.d: 30 days

distractorExplanations.a: 10 days would follow from three tablets daily (TID); the sig is one tablet once daily.
distractorExplanations.b: 15 days would follow from two tablets daily (BID); the sig is one tablet once daily.
distractorExplanations.c: 28 days treats the fill as a four-week calendar pack; 30 tablets at one daily is a 30-day supply.

options.a: Substitute generic if state law permits and profile allows; otherwise contact prescriber
options.b: Dispense brand Coumadin, because warfarin is a narrow-index drug barred from substitution
options.c: Substitute generic warfarin and adjust the strength to the closest tablet currently stocked
options.d: Hold the prescription until the prescriber sends a new order written for generic warfarin

distractorExplanations.b: Narrow-therapeutic-index status may add state conditions, but AB-rated generic warfarin is not federally barred from substitution.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitution changes the manufacturer, never the strength; altering the 5 mg dose needs prescriber authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: A brand-name order without DAW already permits generic substitution where state law allows; a new order is not required.

options.a: Submit the claim anyway, since a pending PA lets the plan pay once it is approved
options.b: Inform patient/pharmacist, explore covered alternatives, and follow PA workflow
options.c: Switch the patient to a generic equivalent on your own while the PA is still pending
options.d: Tell the patient to request the PA directly from the insurer before you take action

distractorExplanations.a: A claim submitted before PA approval rejects; plans do not hold and pay a claim retroactively just because a PA is pending.
distractorExplanations.c: The drug is brand-only, and technicians cannot change therapy; alternatives go through the pharmacist and prescriber.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong party: prior authorization is submitted by the prescriber's office, not requested by the patient.

options.a: The patient requested the brand product, so generic substitution is not allowed
options.b: Brand is dispensed because a generic is not available in the marketplace
options.c: Dispense the brand product as written; generic substitution not permitted
options.d: Substitution permitted; the pharmacist chose to dispense the brand product instead

distractorExplanations.a: That describes DAW 2 (patient requested brand), not DAW 1, where the prescriber requires the brand.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes DAW 8 (generic not available in the marketplace), not the prescriber-required brand of DAW 1.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes DAW 3 (pharmacist selected brand); DAW 1 means the prescriber prohibited substitution.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: DAW 1 indicates prescriber requires brand as written. Without a prescriber change, the brand must be dispensed.

options.a: Enter it as 'Take 2 tablespoonfuls by mouth four times daily as needed for pain'
options.b: Enter it as 'Take 2 teaspoonfuls by mouth every four hours as needed for pain'
options.c: Enter it as 'Take 2 teaspoonfuls by mouth four times daily' and leave out PRN
options.d: Translate accurately using standard sigs and verify with pharmacist if unclear

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses tsp (teaspoon, 5 mL) with tbsp (tablespoon, 15 mL), tripling the dose.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses QID (four times daily) with q4h (every four hours), which allows up to six doses a day.
distractorExplanations.c: Dropping PRN turns an as-needed order into scheduled dosing; every element of the sig must be translated.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Accurate sig translation ensures safe use; unclear orders need pharmacist clarification. Use standard abbreviations/sigs per pharmacy policy.

options.a: State law and time from issue date (often 6–12 months)
options.b: The DEA, which limits all prescriptions to six months and five refills
options.c: The manufacturer expiration date printed on the stock bottle
options.d: Federal FDA rules setting a uniform 90-day validity window

distractorExplanations.b: The six-month / five-refill limit is the DEA rule for Schedule III–IV; non-controlled prescription validity is set by state law.
distractorExplanations.c: The stock bottle's expiry governs the drug product, not how long the prescription itself remains valid.
distractorExplanations.d: No federal FDA rule sets a 90-day validity window; non-controlled prescription expiration is a state-law matter.

options.a: Submit using the pharmacy's own NPI in the prescriber field
options.b: Obtain valid prescriber NPI/ID required by payer before billing
options.c: Submit using the prescriber's DEA number in place of the NPI
options.d: Bill the claim now and add the NPI later if the payer rejects it

distractorExplanations.a: The pharmacy NPI identifies the dispenser, not the prescriber; putting it in the prescriber field misrepresents the claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Payers such as Medicare Part D require the prescriber NPI; a DEA number is a controlled-substance registration, not a billing ID.
distractorExplanations.d: Knowingly submitting an incomplete claim invites rejection or audit recoupment; the valid NPI must be obtained before billing.

options.a: Refuse it, since Schedule II partial fills are allowed only when stock runs short
options.b: Partial fill it, with the balance dispensable any time within six months of issue
options.c: Partial fill per federal/state rules with pharmacist approval and documentation
options.d: Partial fill it and issue the remainder as a refill under the same prescription

distractorExplanations.a: Outdated rule: since CARA 2016, a patient or prescriber may request a C-II partial fill, not only when stock is short.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the six-month C-III–V window with Schedule II, where a requested partial balance must be filled within 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: The remaining quantity is a partial fill of the same order, not a refill; Schedule II prescriptions cannot have refills.

options.a: Sign the carrier's receipt and shelve the totes, reconciling the invoice at month-end
options.b: Log each item into perpetual inventory using the quantities printed on the invoice
options.c: Count totes against the carrier manifest and sign for them, then stock the shelves
options.d: Verify shipment against purchase order/invoice, check for damage, and confirm lot/expiry

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying reconciliation to month-end means shortages, damage, and wrong items are found after the claim window closes.
distractorExplanations.b: Posting invoice quantities without a physical count records what was billed, not what actually arrived.
distractorExplanations.c: Counting totes checks the carrier delivery, not the contents; items, damage, and lot/expiry still need verification.

options.a: Use oldest acceptable stock with nearest expiration first
options.b: Place newly received stock in front so it is dispensed first
options.c: Dispense the lot with the latest expiration to lower waste risk
options.d: Use stock in the order it appears on the wholesaler invoice

distractorExplanations.b: This reverses FIFO: new stock goes behind older stock so the older units are used first.
distractorExplanations.c: Dispensing the latest-dated lot first leaves older lots to expire, which increases waste instead of reducing it.
distractorExplanations.d: Invoice line order has no relation to expiration dates; FIFO is based on what was received and expires first.

options.a: Return unopened bottles of the lot but keep opened bottles in use until they run out
options.b: Quarantine affected lot, notify pharmacist, check stock/patient records per recall class
options.c: Pull the lot only if the recall is Class I; Class II and III lots may stay in use
options.d: Wait for the FDA to call patients, since pharmacies do not contact recall recipients

distractorExplanations.a: A recall covers the whole lot, opened or not; opened bottles of lot ABC123 must also be quarantined.
distractorExplanations.c: Recall class sets urgency and depth (e.g., patient level), but Class II and III recalled lots are still removed from stock.
distractorExplanations.d: The FDA does not notify individual patients; pharmacies check dispensing records and contact patients when the recall depth requires it.

options.a: Set the reorder point at the maximum level so orders go out early
options.b: Track controlled substance balances for DEA biennial inventories
options.c: Maintain adequate stock without excessive carrying cost or outages
options.d: Calculate the day supply for third-party prescription claims

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the two settings: the minimum is the reorder point; the maximum caps how much is ordered.
distractorExplanations.b: Controlled-substance balances belong to perpetual and biennial inventory records, not to min/max ordering levels.
distractorExplanations.d: Day supply is a claim calculation from quantity and sig, unrelated to setting stock reorder levels.

options.a: Placed in the refrigerator right away and dispensed once they return to 2–8 °C
options.b: Frozen immediately to stop further degradation, then thawed when needed
options.c: Returned to the carrier unopened without recording the temperature excursion
options.d: Segregated, documented, and referred to pharmacist/manufacturer guidance

distractorExplanations.a: Returning to 2–8 °C does not undo a cold-chain break; vaccines are held and labeled 'do not use' until the manufacturer assesses them.
distractorExplanations.b: Freezing damages many refrigerated vaccines; storage must match the label, and the excursion still needs assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: The excursion must be documented (temperature, duration) for manufacturer guidance; skipping the record loses that data.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Cold chain breaks require quarantine and assessment; compromised vaccines may need discard. Compromised vaccines are likely not dispensed.

options.a: Reconcile physical inventory with computer records on a scheduled basis
options.b: Replace the DEA biennial controlled substance inventory with rolling counts
options.c: Count every item in the pharmacy on one day at fiscal year-end
options.d: Set min/max reorder points based on monthly dispensing volume

distractorExplanations.b: Cycle counts supplement but do not replace the DEA-required biennial inventory of controlled substances.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a full annual physical inventory; cycle counting checks a portion of items on a rotating schedule.
distractorExplanations.d: Setting min/max levels uses usage data; cycle counts verify on-hand quantities against records.

options.a: BX rating in the Orange Book
options.b: AB rating for generic substitution
options.c: An interchangeable code in the Purple Book
options.d: BC rating for extended-release forms

distractorExplanations.a: BX means FDA has insufficient data to establish equivalence; only A-rated (e.g., AB) products are substitutable.
distractorExplanations.c: The Purple Book lists biologics and interchangeable biosimilars; small-molecule generic equivalence is coded in the Orange Book.
distractorExplanations.d: B codes, including BC for extended-release products, mean FDA does not consider them therapeutically equivalent.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: FDA therapeutic equivalence codes (e.g., AB) guide generic substitution eligibility. An AB code applies to generic substitution in many cases.

options.a: Refused at delivery, since product under 90 days to expiry cannot be sold
options.b: Accepted and shelved behind current stock so older lots go out first
options.c: Evaluated against turnover; return or use quickly per policy
options.d: Accepted and labeled with a beyond-use date one year from receipt

distractorExplanations.a: No rule bars selling product within 90 days of expiry; acceptance depends on turnover and policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Shelving the shortest-dated product behind current stock means it expires unused; it should be used first.
distractorExplanations.d: A beyond-use date cannot extend past the manufacturer expiration; a 30-day product cannot get a one-year date.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Short dating increases expiration risk; policy may require return or prioritized dispensing. Prompt return or use avoids waste.

options.a: A physical count of every schedule once a year for the DEA
options.b: Balances updated weekly from the wholesaler purchase history
options.c: Exact counts of all schedules, logged once at month-end
options.d: Running balance updated with each receipt and dispense

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses perpetual inventory with the DEA biennial inventory, which is a count every two years, not a running balance.
distractorExplanations.b: Weekly updates from purchase history miss dispensing in between; a perpetual record changes with every transaction.
distractorExplanations.c: A month-end count is a periodic inventory; perpetual inventory is updated at each receipt and dispense.

options.a: Documented and disposed/returned per policy and DEA/state rules if controlled
options.b: Returned to the wholesaler for credit, with controlled drugs logged on a DEA 222
options.c: Placed in the hazardous-waste bin, with controlled drugs reported on a DEA 106
options.d: Repackaged into a labeled vial and used first if the tablets are still potent

distractorExplanations.b: DEA Form 222 is for ordering or transferring C-I/C-II; destruction of controlled stock is documented on DEA Form 41 or via a reverse distributor.
distractorExplanations.c: DEA Form 106 reports theft or significant loss, not destruction of damaged controlled stock.
distractorExplanations.d: Crushed tablets are adulterated stock; repackaging and dispensing them is not permitted.

options.a: Buying from another pharmacy's surplus without a transaction record
options.b: Secondary vendor ordering per contract and pharmacist approval
options.c: Compounding the commercial product in-house until supply returns
options.d: Holding all orders until the primary wholesaler is restored

distractorExplanations.a: DSCSA requires transaction information and licensed trading partners; undocumented surplus purchases break traceability.
distractorExplanations.c: Compounding copies of commercially available products is restricted and is not a substitute for licensed purchasing.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding every order causes avoidable stockouts; contracts include licensed secondary vendors for outages.

options.a: Record the loss on DEA Form 222 and adjust the balance to match the count
options.b: Recount at the next scheduled biennial inventory before reporting anything
options.c: Notify pharmacist immediately and begin discrepancy investigation per policy
options.d: File DEA Form 106 yourself today and correct the perpetual log to match

distractorExplanations.a: DEA Form 222 is an order form, not a loss report; balances are never adjusted before an investigation.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting up to two years for the biennial count delays a required investigation; C-II discrepancies go to the pharmacist now.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong party and sequence: the pharmacist-in-charge decides whether a Form 106 is needed after investigating the discrepancy.

options.a: Storage under USP <797> sterile compounding area rules
options.b: Locked storage in the C-II safe with the opioid inventory
options.c: Refrigeration in a shared drug fridge to slow degradation
options.d: Segregation and labeling per USP <800> pharmacy practices

distractorExplanations.a: USP <797> covers sterile compounding; hazardous-drug handling and storage are set by USP <800>.
distractorExplanations.b: Cyclophosphamide is not a controlled substance; hazardous drugs are segregated from other stock, not stored with opioids.
distractorExplanations.c: Storage temperature follows the label; shared refrigerators mix hazardous drugs with other stock, which USP <800> seeks to avoid.

options.a: Matching the bottle to the pocket by drug name, skipping the barcode scan
options.b: Verification of drug, strength, lot, expiry, and location scan per policy
options.c: Loading new stock in front of older units so the newest is dispensed
options.d: Restocking by the nurse who removes the drug, without a pharmacy check

distractorExplanations.a: Name matching alone misses wrong strength or form; the barcode scan is the key ADC restock check.
distractorExplanations.c: Placing new stock in front reverses FIFO and leaves older units to expire in the pocket.
distractorExplanations.d: ADC restocking is a pharmacy function with verification; the nurse who removes doses does not restock unchecked.

options.a: Shelving LASA pairs side by side so staff can compare them directly
options.b: Using brand names only on labels so similar generics are not confused
options.c: Tall-man lettering, separate storage, and independent double-checks
options.d: Color-coding by manufacturer so look-alike packages are recognized

distractorExplanations.a: Adjacent storage is a classic cause of LASA picking errors; ISMP recommends separating look-alike pairs.
distractorExplanations.b: Brand names also look and sound alike (e.g., Celebrex/Celexa); dropping generic names removes a safety check.
distractorExplanations.d: Manufacturer colors vary and change; packages from one maker often look more alike, not less.

options.a: Follow the master formula and assign the manufacturer's expiry date as the BUD
options.b: Follow the formula but substitute an available excipient without documenting it
options.c: Compound in the sterile cleanroom hood and assign a USP <797> beyond-use date
options.d: Follow master formula, use calibrated equipment, label beyond-use date, and document

distractorExplanations.a: A compounded preparation gets a USP <795> beyond-use date, not the ingredient manufacturer's expiration date.
distractorExplanations.b: Any ingredient change must follow the formula and be documented on the compounding record.
distractorExplanations.c: Non-sterile compounding follows USP <795>; USP <797> sterile rules and BUDs do not apply to an oral suspension.

options.a: Alert pharmacist immediately, document, and initiate adverse event workflow
options.b: Tell the patient to stop the drug and take diphenhydramine before calling back
options.c: Add a penicillin allergy to the profile and process a refund for the drug
options.d: Submit a MedWatch report yourself and wait for the FDA to respond

distractorExplanations.b: Recommending treatment is clinical counseling outside technician scope; the pharmacist assesses the reaction.
distractorExplanations.c: Recording an allergy before pharmacist assessment skips evaluation of the reaction and next steps for the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: MedWatch reporting may follow, but the immediate step is pharmacist assessment; the FDA does not manage the patient.

options.a: Storage in a locked C-II safe, the same as Schedule II opioids
options.b: Independent double-check of drug, dose, and patient before dispensing
options.c: Dispensing with tall-man lettering on the label in place of a second check
options.d: A second check only when the dose exceeds the usual adult range

distractorExplanations.a: Insulin is high-alert but not controlled; the ISMP safeguard is extra verification, not C-II storage.
distractorExplanations.c: Tall-man lettering is a LASA tool that supports, but does not replace, an independent double-check.
distractorExplanations.d: High-alert drugs are double-checked at every dose; harm can occur at usual doses with the wrong product or patient.

options.a: Wiping the surface from front to back toward the HEPA filter with a dry cloth
options.b: Spraying alcohol directly onto the HEPA filter to disinfect it before the session
options.c: Disinfecting work surface with appropriate agent per USP <797> schedule before session
options.d: Turning on the hood and starting to compound as soon as the blower is running

distractorExplanations.a: Wiping runs back to front, away from the HEPA filter, with a wetted disinfectant; a dry cloth toward the filter spreads particles.
distractorExplanations.b: The HEPA filter must not be sprayed or touched; liquid damages the filter media.
distractorExplanations.d: The hood should run for the manufacturer-specified time and be cleaned before compounding, not used as soon as it starts.

options.a: Left undocumented, since only errors that reach the patient are reported
options.b: Reported to the state board as a dispensing error within 24 hours
options.c: Written up as a disciplinary action in the technician's personnel file
options.d: Documented in internal quality system to prevent recurrence

distractorExplanations.a: Near misses are recorded precisely because they reveal process gaps before harm occurs.
distractorExplanations.b: A near miss did not reach the patient; it is an internal quality event, not a mandatory board-reported dispensing error.
distractorExplanations.c: Just-culture quality systems treat near misses as system data; punitive write-ups discourage reporting.

options.a: Oral syringe calibrated in mL
options.b: A household measuring teaspoon
options.c: A dosing cup marked in drams
options.d: A dropper from another product

distractorExplanations.b: Household spoons vary widely in volume and cause pediatric dosing errors; ISMP recommends mL oral syringes.
distractorExplanations.c: Drams are an apothecary unit ISMP advises against; dosing devices should be marked in mL only.
distractorExplanations.d: Droppers are calibrated for their own product and concentration; reusing one for another liquid gives wrong doses.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Oral syringes in milliliters provide accurate pediatric dosing per best practice. Household teaspoons alone are not accurate enough.

options.a: Absorbent towels and a bleach wipe, with gloves needed only for large spills
options.b: Spill kit, PPE, ventilation considerations, and trained personnel per HD protocol
options.c: Diluting the spill with water first, then mopping it into the regular trash
options.d: Evacuating the pharmacy and waiting for the local fire department to clean up

distractorExplanations.a: Hazardous-drug spills of any size need full PPE (double chemo gloves, gown) from a spill kit, not gloves for large spills.
distractorExplanations.c: Diluting spreads the hazardous drug, and HD waste goes in designated hazardous containers, not regular trash.
distractorExplanations.d: Trained pharmacy staff manage HD spills with a spill kit; fire department response is not the standard protocol.

options.a: Drug-drug interactions without pharmacist review
options.b: Insurance rejections for non-formulary products
options.c: Dosing errors from incorrect sig translation
options.d: Wrong drug/strength/form dispensed to wrong patient

distractorExplanations.a: Interaction screening is a DUR software and pharmacist function; barcode scanning matches product to prescription.
distractorExplanations.b: Formulary rejections come from claim adjudication, which barcode scanning of the product does not affect.
distractorExplanations.c: Barcodes confirm the product, not the typed directions; sig errors are caught at pharmacist verification.

options.a: Stability data, USP standards, and pharmacy policy
options.b: The source container's manufacturer expiry date
options.c: A fixed one-year date for all repackaged solids
options.d: Six months from repackaging, as for compounded solids

distractorExplanations.b: Manufacturer expiry applies to the sealed original container; once repackaged, a BUD must be assigned and may be shorter.
distractorExplanations.c: One year is a ceiling under USP repackaging guidance, not a fixed date; it must also not exceed the source expiry.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses repackaging with compounding; six-month BUDs come from USP <795> for certain compounded preparations.

options.a: Pharmacist notification and correction of the record, with no patient contact if unharmed
options.b: An internal report only, since patients are told about errors when harm results
options.c: Reporting to the state board within 24 hours and suspending the technician involved
options.d: Internal report, pharmacist notification, patient communication, and possible external reporting

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure to the patient is expected even without apparent harm; delayed effects may still need monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Patient communication is required for errors that reach the patient, not only when harm results.
distractorExplanations.c: Board reporting depends on state rules and severity, and suspension is a punitive step outside a quality-improvement process.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Errors require disclosure per policy, documentation, and quality improvement even without harm. External reporting follows pharmacy policy.

options.a: Washing/sanitizing before compounding, after gloves, and after contamination
options.b: Washing at the start of each shift, with gloves covering any later contact
options.c: Sanitizing after handling cash, with gloves replacing washing before compounding
options.d: Washing only after visible soiling, using alcohol rub at all other times

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are cleaned before compounding and after glove removal throughout the shift.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves are worn after hand hygiene, not instead of it; compounding requires washing first.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand hygiene is tied to tasks (compounding, glove removal, contamination), not only to visibly soiled hands.

options.a: Allow up to five refills within six months of the date of issue
options.b: Require original prescription (with e-Rx exceptions) and have no refills
options.c: May be phoned in for any patient if a written copy follows in 30 days
options.d: Allow refills once the 90-day multiple-prescription supply runs out

distractorExplanations.a: Five refills within six months is the Schedule III–IV rule; Schedule II prescriptions cannot be refilled.
distractorExplanations.c: Oral C-II orders are allowed only in emergencies, for a limited quantity, with the written prescription due within 7 days.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiple C-II prescriptions (up to a 90-day supply) are separate prescriptions, not refills; C-II still has no refills.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Federal rules limit Schedule II: no refills, strict prescription requirements. Partial-fill rules are separate from refills.

options.a: Any family member who can state the patient's date of birth and address at pickup
options.b: The patient's employer when the drug affects fitness for work
options.c: Patient's authorized caregiver/designee when documented and necessary for care
options.d: Another pharmacy's staff calling for marketing or loyalty enrollment

distractorExplanations.a: A date of birth verifies identity, not authorization; family members get PHI only when involved in care or authorized.
distractorExplanations.b: Employers are not covered recipients for treatment; disclosure needs the patient's written authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: Marketing use of PHI needs patient authorization; treatment-related pharmacy-to-pharmacy sharing is a different purpose.

options.a: Confront the patient and keep the forged prescription until police arrive
options.b: Fill a three-day supply and let the pharmacist sort it out on the next shift
options.c: Call the prescriber's number printed on the prescription to verify it
options.d: Notify pharmacist, refuse fill, document, and contact authorities per policy

distractorExplanations.a: Confronting the patient risks safety and skips the pharmacist; escalation follows pharmacy policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Dispensing any amount of a suspected forgery is unlawful; the pharmacist must assess it now.
distractorExplanations.c: A forged prescription may list a fake phone number; verification uses an independently sourced prescriber number.

options.a: Offer to counsel Medicaid patients on new prescriptions
options.b: Counsel every patient on every refill, including cash-paying patients
options.c: Keep pseudoephedrine sales logs for every Medicaid patient
options.d: Dispense generics to all Medicaid patients unless DAW is written

distractorExplanations.b: OBRA '90 requires an offer to counsel Medicaid patients; mandatory counseling on every refill for all patients is not the federal rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Pseudoephedrine logbooks come from the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005, not OBRA '90.
distractorExplanations.d: Generic substitution is governed by state law and payer rules; OBRA '90 addresses DUR, patient profiles, and counseling.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: OBRA mandates Medicaid counseling offers and patient profile reviews by pharmacists. Technicians support this workflow.

options.a: The DEA, which licenses technicians to handle controlled drugs
options.b: State board of pharmacy regulations and supervising pharmacist
options.c: The PTCB or NHA certification body that issued the credential
options.d: Federal FDA rules that apply uniformly in every state

distractorExplanations.a: The DEA registers pharmacies and prescribers, not technicians; technician duties are set by state boards.
distractorExplanations.c: Certification bodies test competence but do not set legal scope; state boards of pharmacy do.
distractorExplanations.d: The FDA regulates drugs, not pharmacy practice; technician scope varies by state.

options.a: A prescription in every state under the Combat Methamphetamine Act
options.b: ID and a logbook, with a daily limit of 9 grams per purchaser
options.c: Compliance with federal/state log limits, ID, and quantity restrictions
options.d: Logbook entry, with ID checked for purchases over 3.6 grams

distractorExplanations.a: The federal CMEA sets behind-the-counter limits and logs; only some states require a prescription.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the federal limits: 3.6 g per day and 9 g per 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: ID is checked for every pseudoephedrine sale; 3.6 g is the daily purchase limit, not an ID threshold.

options.a: Enter new prescriptions into the pharmacy computer system
options.b: Take refill requests for non-controlled drugs by phone
options.c: Count and pour controlled substances for pharmacist review
options.d: Perform final clinical verification independently

distractorExplanations.a: Data entry of new prescriptions is a core technician task, subject to pharmacist verification.
distractorExplanations.b: Refill requests are routine technician work; new verbal orders are what states reserve for pharmacists.
distractorExplanations.c: Technicians may count controlled substances; the pharmacist verifies the final product.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: Final verification/clinical check is pharmacist responsibility in most jurisdictions. Tech-check-tech exceptions exist only where state law allows them.

options.a: Ordering Schedule I and II controlled substances from suppliers
options.b: Reporting theft or significant loss of controlled substances
options.c: Documenting destruction of expired controlled substances
options.d: Ordering Schedule III–V controlled substances from suppliers

distractorExplanations.b: Theft or significant loss is reported on DEA Form 106, not Form 222.
distractorExplanations.c: Destruction is documented on DEA Form 41 (or by a reverse distributor), not Form 222.
distractorExplanations.d: Schedule III–V are ordered with an invoice or standard purchase order; Form 222/CSOS is for C-I and C-II.

options.a: Answering at the counter, since HIPAA allows incidental disclosures of any PHI
options.b: Moving to private counseling area and lowering voice/minimum necessary disclosure
options.c: Asking the patient to sign a HIPAA authorization before any discussion
options.d: Referring the question to the prescriber, since pharmacies cannot discuss PHI

distractorExplanations.a: Incidental disclosures are permitted only when reasonable safeguards are used; a loud counter conversation is not safeguarded.
distractorExplanations.c: Discussing a patient's own care with them is a treatment disclosure that needs no signed authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: Pharmacies may discuss a patient's PHI with the patient; the issue is privacy, not referral.

options.a: Placed in the pharmacy's patient take-back collection receptacle
options.b: Destroyed on site by the technician and logged on DEA Form 106
options.c: Disposed through authorized reverse distributor per regulations
options.d: Flushed down the sink with a witness, as with expired liquids

distractorExplanations.a: Collection receptacles are for patients' drugs only; registrants may not put their own inventory in them.
distractorExplanations.b: Form 106 reports theft or loss; destruction is a DEA Form 41 process with authorized witnesses, not a technician task.
distractorExplanations.d: Sewering pharmaceuticals is generally prohibited, and the EPA hazardous waste rule bans sewering hazardous pharmaceuticals.

options.a: Required only after you have personal proof of theft on camera
options.b: Handled by confronting the coworker privately before telling anyone
options.c: A matter for the DEA alone, reported directly without telling the pharmacist
options.d: Ethical/legal obligation to notify pharmacist/owner and possibly board/DEA

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting is based on reasonable suspicion; investigation, not the reporting employee, establishes proof.
distractorExplanations.b: Confronting the coworker can tip off diversion and compromise the investigation; report through proper channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrong order: the pharmacist or owner is notified first and handles DEA and board reporting.

options.a: Valid veterinarian prescription meeting state/federal requirements
options.b: A veterinary prescription, with controlled drugs exempt from DEA rules
options.c: A prescription from any licensed prescriber, including a nurse practitioner
options.d: An order from a veterinary technician working under a veterinarian

distractorExplanations.b: Veterinarians prescribing controlled substances need DEA registration; the usual controlled-substance rules still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Human-health prescribers such as nurse practitioners are not licensed to prescribe for animals.
distractorExplanations.d: Veterinary technicians cannot prescribe; the order must come from the licensed veterinarian.

options.a: OSHA hazard communication standards
options.b: The Poison Prevention Packaging Act
options.c: Anti-kickback and state unfair trade/ethics rules
options.d: The Durham-Humphrey Amendment on legend drugs

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA hazard communication covers workplace chemical hazards, not patient inducements.
distractorExplanations.b: The PPPA requires child-resistant packaging; it does not address inducements to switch prescriptions.
distractorExplanations.d: Durham-Humphrey created the legend/OTC distinction and refill authorization, not rules on gifts to patients.

options.a: Release records only after the prescriber signs off on the request
options.b: Provide records within 90 days, charging the patient's usual copay
options.c: Mail records to the address on file, with no identity check needed
options.d: Provide access per HIPAA/state law with identity verification

distractorExplanations.a: The HIPAA right of access belongs to the patient; prescriber approval is not required.
distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA requires action within 30 days (one 30-day extension) and a reasonable cost-based fee, not a copay.
distractorExplanations.c: Identity verification is required before releasing PHI, whatever the delivery method.

pharmacy-technician-excpt-readiness-chec.explanation: HIPAA grants patients access rights with verification and permitted fees/process. The process must be reasonable.
